title: Accuracy of an automated urgent-message flag for patient portal messages across three primary care clinics
subtitle: Diagnostic accuracy study before switching the flag on
statement: Portal messages to clinicians have risen by about 70 percent since 2023 in a three-clinic primary care organisation, and clinicians spend a median of 1.4 hours a day on them. Urgent messages wait in the same queue as routine requests. The vendor's automated triage flag could route urgent messages faster, but its accuracy in these clinics, and for older patients and messages in languages other than English, is unknown. A diagnostic accuracy study with the flag in silent mode against a two-clinician reference standard is needed before it is switched on.
whoAffected: About 38,000 patients who use the portal, especially older patients, carers and people writing in languages other than English; physicians and nurse practitioners; reception teams.
whatHurts: Urgent messages can wait hours; clinicians work after hours; a flag that misses urgent messages could delay care for the patients least well served.
currentPractice: All messages enter one queue, sorted by reception staff; clinicians read them between and after appointments.
whyNow: The vendor offers the flag, message volume is still rising, and the organisation must decide whether to switch it on in 2027.
constraints: Quality budget of 12,000. Informatics nurse 1 day per week and reviewing clinicians 2 hours per week each until June 2027. The triage flag may run only in silent mode; no clinical action on its output during the study.
patientCenteredGoal: Patients who write about something urgent reach a clinician the same day, whatever their age or language.
summary: Problem framed as a multi-site diagnostic accuracy study of a message triage flag.
